token_equality.reconstruction: ordinary_forward input_token IDs, followed by final ordinary_forward next_token; validated 32-token list cases only.

graph_history.status: Inferred from cold prompt lengths, ordinary-forward positions and model.rs graph policy, not direct cache instrumentation. max_batch=128, dump=false, all_logits=false; 97 command buffers per graph per GPU.

conclusions: Full 19-request cold replay reproduces the anomaly: greedy short requests are 4.915 and 5.979 seconds after 1.821/1.678-second stochastic short requests. Fresh short cold and cached five-request sequences do not reproduce it.

All 32 emitted list token IDs match across the 12 short cold, cached and full-replay stochastic/greedy responses. Workload, output length and hidden reasoning are not explanations for this comparison.

Direct measured bottleneck is distributed time between GPU timestamped segments. Mean shader work stays about 35.6 ms while per-card summed gaps rise to 98–142 ms per forward. Host wait absorbs the delay; shader work, host submission and reads do not.

All sampled clocks during the four relevant full-replay short requests are 850/1370 MHz on both cards. Peak sampled temperatures are 82/80 C. This does not prove clocks never briefly change between samples, but a clock or shader-throughput explanation cannot account for the observed unchanged kernel times.

Long-context greedy requests immediately after the slow short requests return to about 3 ms summed gaps, while later short/tool requests again have large gaps. Evidence points to graph-/history-dependent driver submission or synchronization behavior, not a global sustained compute slowdown.

The first slow short greedy decode graph is newly recorded after long and stochastic graphs. Simple reuse of an old short greedy graph cannot by itself explain onset. Graph cache/command-pool residency and persistent queue/timeline/imported-buffer synchronization state remain unseparated hypotheses.

CPU PM QoS request 0 us is confirmed in server.log and held by latency-run.py while its subprocess runs. No per-request CPU utilization, OS scheduling trace, memory-pressure or command-buffer placement telemetry was captured.

next_diagnostics.change: Diagnostic-only explicit free/drain of all target cached command buffers at each sampler top-k transition, before prefill. Preserve target GPU buffers, descriptors, query pools, semaphores, counter and KV. Wait for both devices idle before freeing, and record old/new key counts. Retain current per-forward timing.
next_diagnostics.reason: Keeps exact full19 request order and long workload, while removing the prior graph/command-pool residency at transitions into stochastic and greedy. Merely HashMap::clear leaks commands because Graph has no Drop; use the explicit Engine::drop-style free_command_buffers loop.
next_diagnostics.interpretation: Recovery of subsequent steady forwards supports graph/command-pool residency or stale command references; persistence points toward queue/timeline/buffer state or another process-history effect. Extra first-forward recording time is expected; compare GPU gaps and forwards after the first, not just total HTTP wall.

next_diagnostics.change: If transition clearing recovers performance, repeat with device_wait_idle only (retain graphs) to separate queue drain from command freeing. If needed, clear only unneeded graphs rather than all graphs in a follow-up diagnostic.
next_diagnostics.reason: The initial cache-clear diagnostic otherwise changes both cache residency and an explicit device idle operation.

next_diagnostics.change: If clearing does not recover, force target top-k=64 for greedy sampling in the diagnostic build and replay the same full19 bodies, still using argmax CPU sampling. A separate prewarm-short-greedy-before-long sequence can distinguish graph allocation/creation order from later execution history.
next_diagnostics.reason: Fast top-64 and slow top-1 graphs process exactly the same tokens at the same positions. This changes graph identity and only the output-selector specialization, isolating the association without claiming top-k compute is the bottleneck.

interpretation: Freeing cached graphs on top-k transitions restores full-replay greedy #10/#11 from 4.915/5.979 s to 1.666/1.701 s. Mean gaps restore from 97.835/141.975 ms to 3.132/4.084 ms on GPU0.

Visible VRAM does not shrink on free: driver command-buffer storage remains pooled and reused. First four graph allocations consume visible VRAM to 222.25/229.574 MiB; each further graph initially adds exactly 9.09375 MiB per card in this batch128 experiment.

Later graph shapes regrow the pool. GPU1 reaches 255.996 MiB at request15, both cards reach approximately 256 MiB at request16; request16 develops 85 ms gaps. This is strong evidence consistent with visible-VRAM capacity/residency pressure, not a direct allocation-placement trace.

Even after a later 11-key free, short stochastic #21/#22 are slow at 5.129/5.331 s with 112.7/119.4 ms GPU0 gaps; subsequent greedy is fast. This rules out a greedy-only top-k arithmetic explanation and shows late clearing does not ensure a previously grown command pool returns to fast placement.

Enforcing a small graph bound before recording new graphs is the supported next intervention. Its production cap and wider batch buffers still require independent full validation and memory capture; this diagnostic establishes neither an exact universal threshold nor the precise driver-internal mechanism.
